title: trataka
hook: no candle, no mark on the wall: the Gita puts the point of the gaze on the body itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka met its neighbor darshan: the gaze on a sacred image, seeing and being seen. When you greeted someone, did you give them one full, unhurried look? Day one thousand thirty-one.

A train late at night. The carriage is half empty, the lights are harsh, and there's nothing to look at. No candle. No picture. No mark on the wall that isn't an advertisement. A woman across the aisle sits upright with her eyes half lowered, very still, as if looking at nothing in particular, and she stays that way for three stops. Where are her eyes? Trataka so far has needed something out there to look at. The Bhagavad Gita, describing a person in meditation, puts the point of the gaze somewhere you never have to pack.
screen: `A LATE TRAIN. NOTHING TO LOOK AT.` → `EYES HALF LOWERED, VERY STILL.` → `A POINT YOU NEVER HAVE TO PACK.`

segments.voice: In chapter six, Krishna describes how a person sits to meditate. A clean place, a seat neither too high nor too low. And then the body, in paraphrase: holding the body, head and neck straight and still, gazing at the tip of one's own nose, and not looking around in any direction. That last part matters. Not looking around. The verse isn't only about where the eyes go. It's about where they don't go. In chapter five there's a second spot. Krishna describes the sage who shuts out outside contacts, fixes the gaze between the brows, and evens out the breath moving through the nostrils. The tip of the nose. The point between the brows. Two places on the body itself. Later yoga teachers give these gazes names: nasikagra drishti, the gaze at the nose tip, and bhrumadhya drishti, the gaze between the eyebrows. Some count them as forms of trataka, a trataka with no object but the body. Commentators have wondered how literally to read the first one. The teacher Shankara, in his commentary on the Gita, reads it as if looking at the tip of the nose: eyes lowered and resting, not literally crossed. What matters is that the eyes stop roaming. Here's what this adds. Trataka on a flame trains the eyes on a point outside. The Gita's gaze brings the point home. The eyes rest on something that's always with you, on a train, in a waiting room, in bed at night. Teachers add a caution: soft eyes, never strain, and stop if the eyes ache.
screen: `BODY, HEAD, NECK STRAIGHT AND STILL.` · `THE NOSE TIP, AND NOT LOOKING AROUND.` · `BETWEEN THE BROWS, BREATH EVENED OUT.` · `AS IF LOOKING: EYES LOWERED, RESTING.` · then, large: `A POINT YOU CARRY EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, with the head and neck easy and straight. Let the eyes lower, half closed, and let them rest as if looking toward the tip of the nose. No crossing, no strain. Just stop the roaming. If the eyes feel comfortable, after a while you can lift the soft gaze toward the space between the brows, eyes closed if that's easier. Notice the breath moving evenly at the nostrils. If anything aches, let the eyes simply close and rest. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, the point moves onto the body: the tip of the nose, the space between the brows.
Your line: trataka. Today, somewhere with nothing to look at, a ride or a long wait, lower the eyes, let them rest, and stop the roaming until something calls you back. Day one thousand thirty-one.

howItsDone: In some schools of yoga, practitioners rest a soft, half-lowered gaze toward the tip of the nose or the point between the brows during meditation, following the Gita's descriptions, and some teachers call these forms of trataka.

Shankara reads it as if looking at the nose tip: eyes lowered and resting, not literally crossed.
the Gita's verse also says not to look around in any direction
in chapter six, the gaze at the nose tip comes with not looking around.

fork.setup: you're sitting as the Gita's chapter six describes: body, head and neck straight. where do the eyes go?
options: around the room, taking it in.
toward the tip of your own nose, not looking around.
fork.reveal: Krishna describes gazing at the tip of one's own nose and not looking around. Shankara reads it as eyes lowered, as if looking there.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: nasikagra, the tip of the nose. Where the Gita's meditator rests the gaze in chapter six.

trapdoor: what you thought: trataka needs a candle.
what it means: the Gita puts the gaze on the body itself, the nose tip or between the brows.
what a scholar hears: Gita 6.13, saṃprekṣya nāsikāgraṃ svaṃ, 5.27 on bhruvor antare, and Shankara's 'as if' reading.
